strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: user-level privacy for federated speech recognition. Speaker-partitioned Common Voice data and LibriSpeech-to-Common-Voice adaptation provide useful benchmarks for heterogeneity and domain shift.

The empirical investigation is extensive, covering three languages, seed models, cohort sizes, optimizers, normalization, and data heterogeneity. The transferable training configurations and strong results with pretrained seeds provide useful practical knowledge.

Per-layer clipping produces a substantial improvement at matched noise and overall clipping bounds: Table 2 reports English test WER decreasing from 31.1% with global clipping to 21.2% with uniform per-layer clipping and 20.4% with dimension-based clipping. Establishing when an existing technique becomes effective is a valuable empirical contribution.

The manuscript provides substantial preprocessing, training, ablation, and compute details. It explicitly labels extrapolated results and states the public-data assumption for nonprivate pretraining. The use of public research datasets raises no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The central privacy–utility claim is not demonstrated at the evaluated population size. In Table 2, the experiment underlying the headline epsilon=7.2 result actually has 34,753 users, a cohort of 1,024, and reported epsilon approximately 1.2×10^8. Epsilon=7.2 requires extrapolation to approximately 69.5 million users and cohorts of 204,800, assuming comparable WER without validating that assumption. Although transparently disclosed, this leaves the principal capability unsupported. A measured privacy–utility curve at meaningful epsilon values and empirical validation of the scaling assumption are needed.

The privacy theorem needs a precise match to the implemented mechanism. Algorithm 1 specifies independent client sampling, switches to fixed-size cohorts in practice, and normalizes by the realized cohort size; Theorem 1 instead uses sensitivity C/(qN) with sampled-Gaussian accounting. These differences require justification or corrected sampling, normalization, and accounting before the stated guarantees can be accepted.

The claim of nearly optimal performance, including training from scratch, is too broad. Table 4 reports 25.7% test WER for training from scratch on CV English at the largest evaluated cohort, versus 18.2% centrally. The headline 1.3-percentage-point privacy penalty also uses the nonprivate FL baseline of 19.1%; the corresponding central baseline is 17.8%. These comparisons should be stated consistently.

The proposed explanation and generality of per-layer clipping remain incomplete. The main text emphasizes attention-layer vulnerability, whereas Appendix D.5 identifies MLP parameters as most sensitive to noise. Table 17 shows only 0.2- and 0.1-point improvements for French and German at the compared noise level. These findings warrant reconciling the mechanism and narrowing claims that per-layer clipping is essential for large transformers generally.

Practicality and reproducibility remain limited. Millions of participating users with transcribed speech do not establish feasibility for low-resource languages, and GPU simulations provide no device-memory or communication measurements for full 255M-parameter training. Code release is only promised, and repeated-run uncertainty is not reported, making the smaller ablation gains difficult to assess. Together with the unvalidated privacy extrapolation, these shortcomings outweigh the substantial benchmarking merits.
